'''''Pandorea pandorana''''', commonly known as the '''wonga wonga vine'''<ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Quirico |first1=Anna-Louise |title=''Pandorea pandorana'' |url=https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Pandorea~pandorana |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=21 October 2021}}</ref> or '''wonga-vine''',<ref name="RBGV">{{cite web |last1=Jeanes |first1=Jeff A. |title=''Pandorea pandorana'' |url=https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/9c415aca-0d80-4257-b39f-125949b00342 |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria |access-date=21 October 2021}}</ref> is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Bignoniaceae]] and is native to Australia, [[Malesia]] and the southwestern [[Pacific Islands|Pacific]] region. It is a woody scrambler or climber with [[Pinnation|pinnate]] leaves, juvenile leaves differing from those of mature plants. The flowers are tubular or funnel-shaped and white with purple markings and the fruit are [[Capsule (fruit)|capsules]] containing winged seeds. It is easy species to germinate and is a popular garden plant. Common cultivars include the yellow-flowered ''P.'' 'Golden Showers', the white-flowered ''P.'' 'Snowbells', and the pinkish ''P.'' 'Ruby Belle'. The wood was used in making spears for [[Woomera (spear-thrower)|woomeras]] in the Central and Western deserts.
[[File:Pandorea pandorana mygarden.jpg|thumb|White form (''Pandorea'' 'Snow Bells')]]

==Description==
''Pandorea pandorana'' is a [[wikt:glabrous|glabrous]] woody climber or scrambler, sometimes reaching a height of {{cvt|6|m}} or more. The leaves are arranged in opposite pairs and pinnate, those of juvenile plants {{cvt|20–80|mm}} long with eight to seventeen wavy-edged leaflets. Adult leaves have mostly three to nine egg-shaped leaflets on a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{cvt|10–45|mm}} long, the leaflets {{cvt|25–80|mm}} long and {{cvt|5–30|mm}} wide on [[Petiole (botany)|petiolules]] {{cvt|1–2|mm}} long.<ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="RBGV" /><ref name="Les">{{cite book |last1=Robinson |first1=Les |title=Field guide to the native plants of Sydney |date=1991 |publisher=Kangaroo Press |location=Kenthurst, NSW |isbn=0864171927 |page=328}}</ref><ref name="anpsa">{{cite web |title=''Pandorea pandorana'' |url=http://anpsa.org.au/p-pan.html |publisher=Australian Native Plants Society (Australia) |access-date=21 October 2021}}</ref><ref name="ATRP">{{cite web |title=''Pandorea pandorana'' (Andrews) Steenis |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/rainforest/text/entities/pandorea_pandorana.htm |author=F.A. Zich |author2=B.P.M Hyland |author3=T. Whiffen |author4=R.A. Kerrigan |website=[[Australian Tropical Rainforest Plants]], Edition 8 |year=2020 |publisher=[[Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation]] (CSIRO) |access-date=21 October 2021}}</ref>

The flowers are arranged in groups up to {{cvt|220|mm}} long with several to many [[thyrse]]s. The flowers are pendent, tubular or funnel-shaped, each on a [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]] {{cvt|2–8|mm}} long and white to cream-coloured with purple markings. The [[sepal]]s are {{cvt|3–5|mm}} long and joined at the base with lobes about {{cvt|1|mm}} long. The petal tube is {{cvt|10–25|mm}} long, the tubular part more or less straight and {{cvt|5–10|mm}} in diameter, bearded on the inside, the lobes {{cvt|3–6|mm}} long. Flowering occurs from June to December followed in summer by oblong capsules {{cvt|4–6|mm}} long and {{cvt|10–20|mm}} wide containing a large number of winged seeds.<ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="RBGV" /><ref name="ATRP" />

==Taxonomy==
[[File:Tab 5 Vol 1 Annales Musei Botanici Lugduno-Batavi.jpg|thumb|''Pandorea pandorana'' subsp. ''pandorana'' illustrated in ''Annales Musei Botanici Lugduno-Batavi''.]]
Wonga wonga vine was first formally described in 1800 by English botanist [[Henry Cranke Andrews]] who gave it the name ''Bignonia pandorana'' in ''The Botanist's Repository for New, and Rare Plants'' from specimens grown in London by [[Lee and Kennedy]] from seed collected on [[Norfolk Island]] by [[William Paterson (explorer)|Colonel Paterson]].<ref name=APNI1>{{cite web|title=''Bignonia pandorana''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/456930 |publisher=APNI|access-date=21 October 2021}}</ref><ref name="Andrews">{{cite book |last1=Andrews |first1=Henry Cranke |title=The Botanist's Repository for New, and Rare Plants |date=1800 |volume=2 |location=London |page=86 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/109209#page/29/mode/1up |access-date=21 October 2021}}</ref> In 1928 [[Cornelis Gijsbert Gerrit Jan van Steenis]] gave the species its present name.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Pandorea pandorana''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/513066 |publisher=APNI|access-date=21 October 2021}}</ref> Both the generic and specific name are derived from the [[Greek mythology|Greek mythological]] woman [[Pandora]].<ref name=EJ97>{{cite book | last1=Elliot | first1=Rodger W. | last2=Jones | first2=David L. | last3=Blake | first3=Trevor |title=Encyclopaedia of Australian Plants Suitable for Cultivation:Volume 7 – N-Po|year=1997|pages=160–61|publisher=Lothian Press |location=Port Melbourne |isbn=0-85091-634-8}}</ref> The Scottish botanist [[Robert Brown (botanist, born 1773)|Robert Brown]] had described it as ''Tecoma australis'' but this name was ruled invalid.<ref name="APNI2">{{cite web|title=''Tecoma australis''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/496760 |publisher=APNI|access-date=21 October 2021}}</ref>

In 1862, [[Louis Édouard Bureau]] formally described ''Tecoma austrocaledonica'' in the ''[[Société botanique de France|Bulletin de la Société botanique de France]]'',<ref name=APNI3>{{cite web|title=''Tecoma austrocaledonica''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/551749 |publisher=APNI|access-date=24 October 2021}}</ref> later reduced to ''Pandorea pandorana'' subsp. ''austrocaledonica'' by [[Peter Shaw Green]], but that name is not accepted by the [[Australian Plant Census]].<ref name=APNI4>{{cite web|title=''Pandorea pandorana subsp. austrocaledonica''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/891383 |publisher=APNI|access-date=21 October 2021}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Gardenology-IMG 5017 hunt10mar.jpg|thumb|Habit]]
A highly variable species, it is found across continental Australia in every state.<ref name=EJ97/> It is also found in [[Indonesia]], [[Papua New Guinea]], the [[Solomon Islands]], [[New Caledonia]] and [[Vanuatu]].<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | accessdate = 12 January 2018}}</ref> It is also found on [[Flinders Island]] in [[Bass Strait]], but not on mainland Tasmania. In New Zealand the species has become naturalised within disturbed native vegetation near parks and gardens in which it is cultivated.<ref>{{cite web|title=''Pandorea pandorana''|work=Weedbusters|url=http://weedbusters.co.nz/weed_info/detail.asp?WeedID=76|accessdate=7 February 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120114161357/http://weedbusters.co.nz/weed_info/detail.asp?WeedID=76|archive-date=14 January 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref>

It occurs in many habitats, from rainforest, to dry sclerophyll forest, to dry scrub and rocky outcrops in arid regions. It can grow in either clay or sand-based soils.

==Uses==
===Uses by Indigenous Australians===
The highly flexible wood of ''Pandorea pandorana'' was the most sought after for use in [[Woomera (spear-thrower)|woomera]]-cast spears among the people of the Central and Western Deserts. Its versatility allowed short pieces to be spliced together if longer ones could not be found.<ref name="RSSA">{{cite journal |last1=Cleland |first1=John B. |last2=Tindale |first2=Norman B. |title=The native names and uses of plants at Haast Bluff, Central Australia |journal=Transactions of the Royal Society of South Australia |date=1959 |volume=82 |page=139 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/127470#page/157/mode/1up |access-date=21 October 2021}}</ref> Due to its cultural significance, a group of mythological women with slender and flexible bodies were named after it.<ref>{{cite book |author=Strehlow TGH |year=1971|title=Songs of Central Australia|publisher = Angus and Robertson|location=Sydney|pages=469}}</ref>

===Use in horticulture===
''Pandorea pandorana'' was first raised in England in 1793 by Lee and Kennedy at their nursery in Hammersmith<ref name="APNI" /> and had flowered in cultivation by 1805. Material was also sent to the garden of the [[Château de Malmaison]] under the auspices of [[Joséphine de Beauharnais]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.jill-hamilton.com/pdf/napoleon-the-empress-and-the-artist.pdf |title=Archived copy |accessdate=2008-09-23 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110713104906/http://www.jill-hamilton.com/pdf/napoleon-the-empress-and-the-artist.pdf |archivedate=2011-07-13 }}</ref> Its floral display makes it a popular and widely grown garden plant. It is an evergreen, half-hardy (hardy to about minus 5 °C once established), twining plant with lovely foliage, particularly so on young plants when it is very finely cut and somewhat fern-like. It is suitable for indoor or outdoor planting. Pruning is necessary to control the quick growing plant, which can overwhelm other plants in a small garden. The plant prefers full-sun to partial shade. It has been argued that the more sun it receives, the more flowers will bloom as a result. The species may be propagated by fresh seed, layering or semi-hardwood tip cuttings.

The Nursery and Garden Industry in Australia promoted ''P. pandorana'' as a native alternative to the invasive garden climber Black-eyed Susan (''[[Thunbergia alata]]'').<ref>{{cite journal |url=http://www.ngia.com.au/publication_resources/NP_Pdf/NP_2001-12.pdf |title=Discovering Alternatives to garden Escapees |accessdate=2008-09-21 |journal=The Nursery Papers|issue=12 |publisher=Nursery and Garden Industry (NGIA) |date=2001 |issn=1326-1495 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080723225718/http://www.ngia.com.au/publication_resources/NP_Pdf/NP_2001-12.pdf <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archivedate = 2008-07-23}}</ref>

===Cultivars===
Several different coloured cultivars are available, including:
*'Golden Showers' - a long-flowering vigorous form with brown-tinted yellow flowers originally selected from a plant growing near [[Kempsey, New South Wales|Kempsey]] on the New South Wales mid-north coast<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.anbg.gov.au/gnp/gnp13/pandorea-pandorana.html |title=Growing Native Plants: ''Pandorea'' 'Golden Showers' |accessdate=2008-09-21 |author=Butler, Geoff |date=1986 |work=Australian National Botanic Gardens Website |publisher=ANBG}}</ref> Initially called "Golden Rain", it was registered by ACRA in 1987.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/acra/descriptions/acc381.html |title=Pandorea 'Golden Showers' |accessdate=2008-09-21 |work=ACRA website |publisher=Australian Cultivar Registration Authority |date=2007}}</ref>
*'Ruby Belle' has a red-pink flower with cream throat
*'Ruby Heart' has a cream-coloured flower with a deep ruby–maroon blotch at the throat
*'Snowbells' - a vigorous cream-white flowered form, with profuse fragrant flowers

==Cultural reference==
[[Judith Wright]] had her poem, "Wonga vine" published in ''[[The Bulletin (Australian periodical)|The Bulletin]]'' on 22 December 1948.<ref name="Wright">{{cite news |last1=Wright |first1=Judith |title=Wonga Vine |url=https://nla.gov.au/nla.obj-550491449/view?partId=nla.obj-550493343#page/n1/mode/1up |access-date=21 October 2021 |work=The Bulletin |date=22 December 1948}}</ref>
